scenario: Today's generative track keeps the already published conversational memory architecture and adds newly surfaced papers. One is Shopify's report on using Semantic IDs for both search and recommendation. The others cover latent reasoning without teacher-written chains of thought, a cascade that spends expensive language-model reranking only where it helps, and sparse-autoencoder steering of generative recommendations by play concepts.

papers.title: Generative Search and Recommendation at Shopify
papers.authors: Juhana Kangaspunta, Khalil Hajji, Darshan Fofadiya, Kyumin Park, Michael Garner, Anthony Maltsev, Ryan Synk, Jose Sepulveda, Joshua Crisologo, Shuying Sun, Akshay Soni
papers.abstract: Search and recommendation at Shopify require retrieving relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of products under strict latency constraints. We present SID-LLM, which casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens representing products. We jointly pre-train SID-LLM on catalog and behavioral data, giving search and recommendation a shared representation and training objective. We show that reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance. Furthermore, distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation quality over joint supervised fine-tuning without a statistically detected loss in search quality. Finally, for efficient serving, we pair multi-token prediction with a lightweight ranker, improving retrieval quality over our autoregressive baseline while reducing latency. We evaluate SID-LLM both as a standalone retriever and as a component of Shopify's production search and recommendation systems. As a standalone search system, SID-LLM achieves quality comparable to Shopify's existing multi-model search stack while meeting production latency requirements. Integrating SID-LLM into the search and recommendation stacks provides significant gains in both offline evaluations and online A/B tests. Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of semantic-ID generation as a unified approach to product discovery at scale.
papers.summary: Search and recommendation at Shopify have to retrieve relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of items under tight latency limits. This report casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens that represent products. The model is jointly pretrained on catalog and behavioral data so search and recommendation share a representation and a training objective. Reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance, and distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation without a statistically detected loss in search quality. In an online test on the home recommendation feed, adding the model raised attributed orders by 7.95%, converting users by 8.60%, and conversion rate by 9.85% on that feed.

papers.title: Rethinking Latent Reasoning for Generative Recommendation: Beyond Teacher-Generated CoT and Recurrent Hidden-State Feedback
papers.authors: Yiwen Chen, Fuwei Zhang, Zehao Chen, Deqing Wang, Hehan Li, Peizhi Xu, Hanmeng Liu, Shuanglong Li, Xin Pei, Fuzhen Zhuang, Zhao Zhang
papers.abstract: Latent reasoning in generative recommendation faces two practical barriers: constructing teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is costly, and recurrent hidden-state feedback requires a specialized execution loop. We revisit both the supervision source and the computation interface. A step-level diagnosis measures how recommendation CoT supports next-item prediction and trace coherence. In the analyzed traces, history analysis is the only step with positive mean contributions on both dimensions, while later preference and intent steps have negative mean answer contributions. Guided by this finding, we propose PHiT (Prefilled, History-Informed Thought Tokens), which learns intermediate states from semantic targets extracted directly from observed item histories. PHiT aggregates cached sparse item encodings to construct these targets and supervises the contextual states of distinct vocabulary thought tokens. All thought tokens are supplied together as ordinary input IDs during a single causal prefill, removing the need for recurrent final-state feedback. With supervised fine-tuning alone, PHiT outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. Controlled ablations support the value of input-matched semantic supervision, while cost measurements show fast target construction with training time comparable to the recommendation-only thought-token baseline.
papers.summary: Latent reasoning for generative recommendation usually needs a teacher model to write chain-of-thought traces, which is costly and hard to stabilize. This paper skips teacher generation. It builds semantic targets from the text meaning of items already in a user's history, and uses those targets to supervise the model's intermediate tokens that are reserved for reasoning steps, without looking at the next-item label. With supervised fine-tuning alone, the method outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. On Beauty, it improves NDCG@1 by 20.6% and NDCG@5 by 10.3% over MiniOneRec. Controlled ablations indicate that the gain comes from input-matched historical semantic supervision, not from extra tokens by themselves.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
papers.summary: Large language models are attractive rerankers, but running an expensive model on every request is costly and often hurts users with short histories. This production system, deployed for content recommendation at a large financial-planning software provider, reranks every request with a lightweight first tier. A router then uses segment cues such as history length to escalate only the requests more likely to benefit to a more expensive second tier, such as a larger model or multi-path reasoning. In a production experiment lasting over a month, it cut inference cost by about 10% versus using the expensive tier uniformly, with little latency impact and no observed quality regression. On MovieLens-1M and Amazon Electronics, uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and the only statistically significant gain appears among users with the longest histories.

papers.title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
papers.authors: Sunkyung Lee, Xiaokai Wei, Da Long, Hyunsik Jeon, Jiajun Wu, Rithwik Seth, Jongwuk Lee, Michelle Gong, Gungor Polatkan
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation aims to predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored. A key challenge is to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change the recommended items. To address this, we propose Steerable Generative Recommender (SteerGR), a framework that uses sparse autoencoders for concept-level control in game discovery. SteerGR proceeds through three stages: (i) Concept Definition and Grounding for defining play concepts with an LLM; (ii) Feature Discovery and Selection for discovering candidate features by their concept associations and selecting one by its steering effect; and (iii) Sparse Feature Intervention for amplifying or suppressing selected features to steer recommendations without retraining the recommender. Extensive experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. We believe this work takes a first step to extend SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders can predict item identifiers from a user's history, but they rarely offer readable, concept-level control over what gets recommended, especially if the model cannot be retrained. This game-discovery work defines play concepts with a language model, finds sparse-autoencoder features that are both associated with a concept and effective when edited, and then amplifies or suppresses those features at inference time. On two industrial generative recommenders, amplification raises the share of the target concept by 113.6% on average for an Atomic ID model and by 24.6% for a Semantic ID model. Selecting features by their steering effect works better than picking the features most strongly associated with the concept.

papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
papers.authors: Emilly Pitman de Castro, Vanessa Silva, Gustavo Kanno, Marcus Santos, Bruno Ferraz do Amaral, Marcelo Nogueira, Lucas Francisco Pellicer, Lucas Lanaro, Pedro Augusto Luiz, João Renato Ribeiro Manesco, Giovanni Carbinatti, Isabela de Lima Santos, Lucas Oliveira Jeronymo, Jeison Fappi, Raul Rotilli Aguirre, Fabio André Frantz, Renata De Paris, Fabiana Marucci, Lohan Silva, Vinicius Diniz Reolon, Wandemberg Gibaut
papers.abstract:
Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level.
In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation.
We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues.
In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure.
Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, retrieving the item a user wants does not mean the user sees it. The authors test this with Amazon review data and simulated users. Each simulated user has a target product in mind but may not name it, so it reveals requirements as the conversation goes. Each turn the system retrieves a batch of candidates and shows only the top 3. By the end of the dialogue the target has been retrieved in 74.75% of sessions, yet only 62.63% of sessions actually put it in front of the user, so the gap sits in choosing which candidates to show. The system itself splits work across several LLM agents: a supervisor asks clarifying questions when the request is vague and brings preferences from the user's earlier sessions into retrieval. Compared with one-shot recommendation, clarification plus memory raised the simulated users' acceptance rate by 28.9 percentage points. When evaluating conversational recommenders, the display step deserves its own measurement.
